topics.title: Values, Values Clarification & Nursing Codes of Ethics
topics.summary: Professional ethics are shared, formal standards that sit above a nurse’s private morals; values clarification and the ANA and ICN codes give the nurse a concrete way to keep personal beliefs from steering client care.
objectives: Distinguish ethics, morality, and law, and classify bedside situations as legal-but-not-moral or moral-but-illegal.
Differentiate values, beliefs, and attitudes and explain how each can shape a nurse’s care without the nurse noticing.
Apply the five AACN professional values (altruism, autonomy, human dignity, integrity, social justice) to concrete nursing behaviors.
Guide a client through values clarification using the seven-step process while remaining neutral.
Respond therapeutically when a client asks, “What would you do?” without imposing personal values.
Identify the purpose and structure of the Nightingale Pledge, the ICN Code of Ethics, and the nine provisions of the ANA Code, and match a nursing action to the correct provision or element.
Choose the safe, ethical action when a co-worker’s practice endangers clients or when a nurse’s personal values conflict with an assignment.
topics.bigPicture:
Every nurse walks onto the unit carrying a lifetime of personal values: family rules, religious teaching, cultural norms, and experiences that taught them what is “right.” Those values are not the problem. The problem is when they quietly decide care: a nurse who believes people with addiction “did it to themselves” assesses pain less carefully, or a nurse who would never refuse chemotherapy pressures a client who wants to. This topic gives you the tools to notice that happening and to replace private judgment with professional standards.

Nursing’s professional standards are written down. The ANA Code of Ethics is nursing’s nonnegotiable ethical standard and its social contract with the public; the ICN Code does the same internationally; the AACN values describe what a professional nurse looks like in action. When the NCLEX gives you an ethically uncomfortable scenario, these documents are what the “right” answer is built on, not what you personally would want.

On the exam, this topic shows up as “What is the nurse’s best response?” when a client asks for your opinion, “Which value is the nurse demonstrating?”, “Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?”, and priority questions about an impaired co-worker or a conflict between your beliefs and your assignment. The winning answers keep the focus on the client, protect safety, stay honest, and use the chain of command.

keyTerms.def: A system of moral principles or standards governing behavior and relationships based on professional nursing beliefs and values; more broadly, standards of right and wrong regarding rights, obligations, benefits to society, fairness, or virtues. Also the study and development of ethical standards of an individual, community, or profession. In nursing, ethics are shared and formal (written in codes).

Private, personal standards of what is right and wrong in conduct, character, and attitude. Moral issues concern important social values and norms, not trivial matters. Clues to a moral situation include feelings of guilt, hope, or shame and words such as ought, should, right, wrong, good, and bad.

Enduring beliefs or attitudes about the worth of a person, object, idea, or action. Values are the foundation for decisions and judgments and develop through cultural, societal, family, and religious experiences.
An interpretation or conclusion a person accepts as true. Beliefs are based more on faith than fact and may or may not be true.
A mental position or feeling toward a person, object, or idea (for example, acceptance, compassion, openness). Attitudes often combine several values and make up a person’s disposition.

The continuous, lifelong process by which people identify, examine, and develop their own values through choosing, prizing, and acting. It helps nurses avoid projecting personal biases onto clients and helps clients make decisions consistent with their own values.
Concern for the welfare and well-being of others; in nursing, concern for the welfare of clients, other nurses, and other health care providers.
The right to self-determination. The nurse respects the client’s right to make health care decisions even when those decisions conflict with what the nurse believes is in the client’s best interest.
Respect for the inherent worth and uniqueness of individuals and populations; the nurse values and respects all clients and colleagues without prejudice or bias.
Acting in accordance with an appropriate code of ethics and accepted standards of practice; the nurse is honest and provides care based on the profession’s ethical framework.

Upholding moral, legal, and humanistic principles by treating all clients equally regardless of economic status, ethnicity, age, gender, religion, citizenship, disability, or sexual orientation, and working to assure equal treatment and access to quality care.

A formal statement of a group’s ideals and values that guides the profession’s members, establishes nonnegotiable ethical standards, and acts as a social contract with the public (for example, the ANA Code of Ethics and the ICN Code of Ethics).

Written in 1893 by Lystra Gretter at the Farrand Training School for Nurses in Detroit and modeled on the Hippocratic Oath; considered the first U.S. nursing code of ethics and still recited at many pinning and graduation ceremonies.

The International Council of Nurses’ code, first adopted in the 1950s, organized around four principal elements that describe nurses’ responsibilities to people, to practice, to the profession, and (in the edition your course uses) to co-workers.

keyTerms.def: The American Nurses Association code (2015 edition in your course) containing nine provisions; nursing’s nonnegotiable ethical standard and social contract with society in the United States.

sections.heading: Ethics, morality, and law: three different rulebooks
sections.body:
Think of these as three overlapping circles. Morality is the personal circle: what you were raised to believe is right or wrong. Ethics is the professional circle: the shared, formal standards nursing has agreed on and written down, such as the duty to protect client privacy or to tell the truth. Law is society’s circle: rules enforced by the government, with penalties.

The three usually agree, which is why it is easy to forget they are separate. The exam tests the places where they do not agree. Laws generally reflect society’s moral values, but an action can be legal but not moral (ordering full resuscitation for a dying client when it only prolongs suffering, which no law forbids) or moral but illegal (speeding to the hospital with a child who has stopped breathing). Professional ethics can also ask more of you than the law does: no statute requires you to sit with a frightened client, but nursing’s ethic of caring does.

Why it matters at the bedside: when your personal morals and professional ethics collide, professional ethics govern your practice. You are allowed to hold your morals; you are not allowed to let them compromise care. A nurse who personally opposes a client’s choice still gives complete information, respects the decision, and, if the conflict is truly unbearable, asks to transfer care through the proper channel instead of refusing or abandoning the client.

check.q: A nurse says, “It is legal for the provider to order another round of aggressive treatment, so it must be the ethical thing to do.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
check.a: Legal and ethical are not the same. An action can be legal but not moral, such as aggressive treatment that only prolongs suffering for a dying client. The nurse must still weigh beneficence, nonmaleficence, and the client’s wishes and advocate if the order conflicts with them.

sections.heading: Values, beliefs, and attitudes: what drives decisions under the surface
sections.body:
Values are enduring ideas about what is worthwhile, such as family, independence, honesty, or health. They are the foundation people use to make decisions. Beliefs are conclusions accepted as true, often more on faith than evidence (“Prayer will heal my infection,” “Vaccines cause autism”); they may or may not be accurate. Attitudes are feelings or mental positions toward a person, object, or idea, such as compassion toward older adults or suspicion toward clients requesting opioids. Attitudes usually combine several values.

The reason the NCLEX cares: values and attitudes leak into care. A nurse who values self-reliance may show impatience toward a client who keeps calling for help. A nurse whose attitude toward people experiencing homelessness is negative may shorten teaching. None of this feels like bias from the inside; it feels like “common sense.” That is why the profession asks nurses to examine their own values deliberately.

Clients’ values matter just as much. A client who values being at work every day may skip appointments; a client who values modesty may refuse a male caregiver; a client who values independence may refuse a walker. Understanding the value behind a choice is what lets the nurse problem-solve with the client instead of labeling the client as “noncompliant.”
sections.example: A client with diabetes repeatedly misses insulin doses at lunch. The nurse’s first impression is that the client “does not care.” On assessment, the client explains that injecting at work is embarrassing and that keeping the job is the most important thing in his life right now. The value (providing for his family) is not the obstacle; the plan is. The nurse collaborates with the provider about regimen options and teaches discreet injection strategies.

check.q: A client states, “My grandmother’s herbal tea will clear my pneumonia; I don’t need antibiotics.” Is this a value, belief, or attitude, and what does it imply for the nurse?
check.a: It is a belief: a conclusion accepted as true, based on faith or tradition rather than evidence. The nurse explores it respectfully, provides accurate information about pneumonia and antibiotics, looks for ways to honor the tradition safely, and respects the informed decision of a client with capacity.

sections.heading: How professional values form and the five AACN values
sections.body:
Professional values are not born; they are built through socialization: observing role models, living through clinical situations, and following institutional policies in school and practice. That is why who you watch as a student matters. The American Association of Colleges of Nursing identified five essential values for the professional nurse. Learn them as behaviors, because the NCLEX describes an action and asks which value it demonstrates.

Altruism is concern for others’ welfare: staying with a frightened client, helping a colleague who is overwhelmed, mentoring a new nurse. Autonomy is respecting self-determination: honoring a capable client’s refusal, presenting all options. Human dignity is respecting each person’s worth: covering a client during a procedure, using the client’s preferred name, caring for a client in police custody with the same respect as anyone else. Integrity is honesty and acting by the code: reporting your own error, documenting accurately, refusing to chart care you did not give. Social justice is fair, equal treatment and access: the same pain assessment for an uninsured client as for an executive, obtaining an interpreter, advocating for clinic access in an underserved area.

Associated professional behaviors include understanding moral, ethical, and legal standards; being accountable for personal and professional behavior; maintaining professional communication with clients, families, and colleagues; providing care free of bias; and embracing lifelong learning.

check.q: A nurse notices that the interpreter phone is often skipped for clients who speak Haitian Creole because “it takes too long,” and she brings the pattern to the unit council. Which AACN value is she demonstrating?
check.a: Social justice: working to assure equal treatment and access to quality care for all clients regardless of language or background. She is advocating at the group level, not only for one client.

sections.heading: Values clarification and the seven-step process
sections.body:
Values clarification is how people identify, examine, and develop their own values through three activities: choosing (freely, from alternatives, after considering consequences), prizing (feeling good about and affirming the choice), and acting (doing something with it, consistently). It is lifelong and continuous.

For the nurse, values clarification is a self-check. Before caring for clients whose choices challenge you (a client who continues to use methamphetamine, a family choosing to withdraw life support, a teen requesting contraception), ask yourself: What do I value here? How might that show up in my tone, my teaching, or how quickly I answer the call light? Recognizing a value does not mean abandoning it; it means preventing it from becoming the client’s burden.

For the client, values clarification helps them make decisions that are consistent with what they actually care about, which increases the chance the plan will be followed. A client who understands that she values seeing her grandchildren grow up may decide differently about smoking cessation than she would after a lecture on lung cancer.

When a client’s values conflict with health care recommendations, the nurse remains neutral. The nurse avoids sharing personal values unless directly asked, and even then briefly answers and immediately redirects the focus back to the client. The seven steps (Al-Banna) give structure to the conversation. Notice that every step is a question to the client, not advice from the nurse.
steps: List alternatives: “What other ways have you thought about handling this?”
Examine possible consequences of choices: “What do you think would happen if you chose that? How do you think that will be helpful?”
Choose freely: “How do you want to make this decision? Do you feel you have a choice?”
Feel good about the choice: “Tell me more about how this choice makes you feel.”
Affirm the choice: “How will you share this decision with your family or the people close to you?”
Act on the choice: “What is your plan for putting this into action?”
Act with a pattern: “Is this the kind of decision you usually make? Would you make the same choice again?”
sections.example: A 68-year-old client with heart failure is deciding whether to have an implanted defibrillator. She asks, “What would you do?” The nurse answers, “What I would choose matters much less than what fits your life. You mentioned you want to travel to see your son; what options have you been weighing?” The nurse has acknowledged the question, declined to steer, and moved to step 1 (list alternatives).

check.q: A client says, “I’ve decided to stop dialysis. Now I need to figure out how to tell my daughters.” Which step of the process is the client working on, and what would the nurse ask?
check.a: Affirm the choice: discussing how the client will communicate the decision to family and significant others. The nurse might ask, “How would you like to share this with your daughters? Would it help to have the team present?”

sections.analogy: Values clarification is like checking your car’s mirrors before changing lanes. The mirrors do not decide where you go; they show you what is in your blind spot so you do not hit anyone. Your personal values are the blind spot; clarification shows them to you before they collide with a client’s choice.

sections.heading: Codes of ethics: Nightingale Pledge, ICN Code, and ANA Code
sections.body:
A code of ethics is a formal statement of a group’s ideals and values. It guides members, sets nonnegotiable standards, and acts as a social contract with the public: society grants nurses trust and the right to practice, and nurses promise to meet these standards.

The Nightingale Pledge (1893) was written by Lystra Gretter at the Farrand Training School for Nurses in Detroit, modeled on the Hippocratic Oath. It is considered the first U.S. nursing code of ethics and is still recited at graduation. The ICN Code of Ethics, first adopted in the 1950s, is organized into four principal elements. The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses with Interpretive Statements has nine provisions and is the standard U.S. nurses are held to.

You do not need to memorize every word. You need to recognize what a nursing action is protecting. Provisions 1–3 are about the client (dignity, primary commitment, advocacy and safety). Provisions 4–6 are about the nurse (accountability, duties to self, the work environment). Provisions 7–9 are about the profession and society (research and standards, collaboration and human rights, social justice through professional organizations).

Promotes, advocates for, and protects the rights, health, and safety of the patient

sections.heading: The ICN Code’s four elements in practice
sections.body:
The ICN Code organizes responsibilities into four principal elements. Nurses and people: the primary responsibility is to people requiring care; respect human rights, values, customs, and spiritual beliefs; hold personal information in confidence; and advocate for equity and social justice for vulnerable populations. Nurses and practice: personal accountability; maintaining personal health so that care is not compromised; using judgment when accepting and delegating responsibility; ensuring technology is compatible with client safety and dignity. Nurses and the profession: implementing clinical, management, research, and education standards; building evidence-based practice; sustaining the natural environment; fostering safe, equitable working conditions. Nurses and co-workers: sustaining collaborative relationships and taking action to safeguard individuals and families when their health is endangered by a co-worker or anyone else.

That last element drives a classic NCLEX priority item. If a co-worker appears impaired, is falsifying records, or is practicing unsafely, protecting clients comes before loyalty to the co-worker. The nurse does not cover for the colleague, does not wait until the end of the shift, and does not confront the colleague in front of clients. The nurse reports through the chain of command (charge nurse or supervisor) immediately so the co-worker is removed from client care, and follows facility policy.
sections.example: At 0650 a nurse notices that the colleague taking report slurs words, smells of alcohol, and fumbles a syringe. Clients are at risk the moment the colleague assumes care. The nurse does not hand off the assignment, notifies the charge nurse immediately, and stays with the clients until the charge nurse reassigns them. Supporting the colleague (referral to employee assistance, alternative-to-discipline programs) is appropriate later; client safety is first.

sections.heading: When your values conflict with your assignment
sections.body:
Nurses sometimes care for clients whose choices violate the nurse’s deeply held moral beliefs (for example, a procedure the nurse’s religion forbids). The ethical path has three parts. First, the client’s autonomy and safety come first: the nurse does not lecture, delay care, or withhold information. Second, if participating would truly violate the nurse’s conscience, the nurse seeks guidance from the supervisor or ethics committee to arrange a safe transfer of care. Third, the nurse never abandons the client: care continues until another qualified nurse accepts the assignment. Ideally, a nurse with known conscientious objections tells the employer in advance, not at the bedside in an emergency.

A conscientious objection covers participation in a specific act; it does not permit a nurse to refuse a whole category of clients (for example, refusing to care for anyone with HIV), which violates human dignity and social justice. In an emergency, the nurse provides life-sustaining care regardless of personal objection.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: values, codes, and the “what would you do?” question
sections.body:
Expect four patterns. (1) Identify the value or provision: a short scenario, then “Which value is demonstrated?” Translate the action into its purpose. (2) Best response when a client asks for your opinion: the right answer redirects to the client’s values and options without advice, reassurance, or refusal to engage. (3) Needs further teaching: a new nurse’s statement about ethics vs morality or about the code; find the statement that lets personal beliefs override care or treats the code as optional. (4) Priority with an unsafe co-worker: client safety first, chain of command, immediate action.

Sample question: A client recovering from a mastectomy says, “My sister had reconstruction and regretted it. Would you have reconstruction if you were me?” Which response by the nurse is best? (A) “Most women in your situation choose reconstruction and are glad they did.” (B) “I can’t give my opinion; you need to ask your surgeon.” (C) “What I would choose matters less than what fits you. What have you been thinking about your options?” (D) “Your sister’s experience doesn’t mean you will feel the same way.”
steps: Read the stem: a client facing a values-based decision directly asks for the nurse’s personal choice.
Identify what is asked: the best therapeutic response that supports autonomy and values clarification.
Spot cues: “if you were me” invites the nurse to substitute her values; the sister’s regret shows the client is weighing consequences.
Eliminate A: it uses bandwagon pressure and steers the decision, imposing values.
Eliminate B: it shuts down the conversation and passes the buck; nurses can explore values and options.
Eliminate D: it dismisses the client’s concern and argues with her rather than exploring it.
Choose C: it briefly acknowledges the question, declines to steer, and redirects to the client’s options (step 1, list alternatives).

check.q: Reusable strategy: what three features does the best answer usually share when a client asks “What would you do?”
check.a: It is honest and brief about the nurse’s role, it returns the focus to the client’s own values, options, or feelings, and it keeps the conversation open with an open-ended question. Eliminate answers that advise, reassure falsely, judge, or refuse to engage.

sections.heading: Worked case: the night nurse and the colleague who “just needs coffee”
sections.body:
You are an RN on a 30-bed medical unit. At 0300 your co-worker, an experienced nurse you admire, asks you to co-sign the wasting of 1 mg of hydromorphone she says she drew up but did not give. You did not see the waste. Earlier you noticed she seemed drowsy and had pinpoint pupils, and two of her clients reported unrelieved pain despite documented doses. She says, “Please, I’m exhausted and need coffee; just sign it.”

This is not a dilemma about friendship; it is a client-safety and integrity problem with clear professional answers.
steps: Recognize cues: request to co-sign a waste you did not witness; drowsiness and pinpoint pupils; clients with unrelieved pain despite documented opioid doses. Together these suggest possible diversion and impairment.
Name the values and code: integrity (you cannot document what you did not see), ANA Provision 3 (protect client health and safety), ICN nurses and co-workers (act when a co-worker endangers health).
Decide: refuse to co-sign. Saying yes would be falsifying a legal record and would leave clients in pain and at risk from an impaired nurse.

Act now through the chain of command: notify the charge nurse or nursing supervisor immediately and state the objective facts; do not confront the colleague in front of clients or investigate on your own.
Protect the clients: reassess the two clients’ pain and notify the provider about unrelieved pain so they receive appropriate treatment.
Document objectively per policy (incident or event report), not in the clients’ medical records as an accusation.
Evaluate: clients are reassigned and reassessed; the colleague is removed from care and referred for evaluation and support. Compassion for her is shown through proper referral, not secrecy.

check.q: Why is “talk to her privately at the end of the shift” the wrong choice?
check.a: It leaves clients exposed to an impaired nurse for hours and delays reporting possible diversion. Client safety and timely chain-of-command reporting come before protecting a colleague’s feelings.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
In North Carolina, nursing is regulated by the North Carolina Board of Nursing (NCBON) under the Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). Codes of ethics are professional standards; the Practice Act and NCBON rules are law. They point the same direction, but only the law carries license consequences. RN components of practice are in 21 NCAC 36 .0224, and the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment.

NCBON uses a Just Culture-based Complaint Evaluation Tool to classify practice events (human error, at-risk behavior, reckless behavior). Conduct issues such as drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud (including falsified documentation), boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches are reported to the Board rather than handled only by the employer. NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses with substance use disorders, which is one way the profession balances accountability with compassion. North Carolina is a Nurse Licensure Compact state, so a multistate license carries these obligations into other compact states.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 44 study guide, pp. 2729–2733 (Master glossary; Outcome 44.1 Values and Ethics in Nursing; Outcome 44.3 Nursing Codes of Ethics, Boxes 44.1 and 44.2).

Clarifications and updates: (1) The five values (altruism, autonomy, human dignity, integrity, social justice) come from the AACN 2008 Baccalaureate Essentials. The 2021 AACN Essentials reorganized competencies into domains (professionalism is Domain 9) but these values remain the core of professional identity and are still tested. (2) The course cites the 2012 ICN Code. The ICN revised its code in 2021; the four elements are now nurses and patients or other people requiring care, nurses and practice, nurses and the profession, and nurses and global health, with co-worker responsibilities folded into the other elements. The duty to act when a co-worker endangers clients is unchanged. (3) The course cites the 2015 ANA Code. ANA has since completed a revision (2025 edition) that keeps the nine-provision structure and the same core commitments; learn the provisions by theme (client, nurse, profession and society), which works for either edition. (4) Conscientious objection: the nurse may request reassignment but must not abandon a client and must provide emergency care.

mnemonics.text: Altruism, Autonomy, Human Dignity, Integrity, Social Justice. The two A’s come first; then the three that protect worth, honesty, and fairness.

mnemonics.name: ANA Code in three blocks: “Client – Nurse – Society”

mnemonics.name: Seven steps: “List, Examine, Choose, Feel, Affirm, Act, Pattern”
mnemonics.text: Say it as “Lucky Elephants Can Fly After Acting Properly.”

pearls: When a client asks “What would you do?”, a short honest acknowledgment followed by an open question about the client’s values beats both giving advice and refusing to talk.
Professional ethics override personal morals in practice; the nurse may hold any belief but may not let it shape the quality of care.
An impaired or unsafe co-worker is a client-safety emergency: report to the charge nurse or supervisor now, not after the shift.
Integrity questions usually involve honesty with records: never chart or co-sign what you did not do or see.
Social justice is about fairness and access for everyone; look for interpreters, equal pain assessment, and advocacy for underserved groups.
A code of ethics is nonnegotiable; any answer treating it as optional when the unit is busy is wrong.
Conscientious objection means requesting reassignment through proper channels while continuing care until relieved.
redFlags: A colleague showing signs of impairment or asking you to co-sign a waste you did not witness.
Your own strong emotional reaction (disgust, anger, judgment) toward a client’s choice: stop and clarify your values before teaching or responding.
Any plan to walk away from a client because of a values conflict without a safe handoff (abandonment).
Care that differs by insurance, race, language, or legal status, which signals a social justice violation.
Pressure from family or staff to steer a capable client toward the “right” decision.
recap: Ethics are shared professional standards; morals are private; law is enforced by society, and the three can conflict.
Values are enduring ideas of worth, beliefs are accepted truths that may be unproven, and attitudes are feelings toward something.
The five AACN values are altruism, autonomy, human dignity, integrity, and social justice; identify them by the action described.
Values clarification (choosing, prizing, acting) protects clients from the nurse’s biases and helps clients choose consistently.
The seven steps run list alternatives, examine consequences, choose freely, feel good, affirm, act, and act with a pattern, and the nurse stays neutral throughout.
The ANA Code (nine provisions) is nursing’s nonnegotiable standard and social contract; the ICN Code is the international equivalent.
Co-worker endangerment means protecting clients first through the chain of command.
A values conflict with an assignment calls for seeking guidance, arranging a safe transfer, and never abandoning the client.

checks.q: A new nurse tells you, “I won’t teach that teen about condoms because I believe abstinence is the only moral choice.” How do you coach her?
checks.a: Her personal morality cannot override professional ethics and the client’s autonomy and right to complete information. She should clarify her values; if she truly cannot provide the teaching, she should tell the charge nurse so another nurse can, without delaying care or shaming the client.

checks.q: A nurse corrects her charting after realizing she documented an assessment before doing it, and tells the charge nurse. Which value is this, and why is it not altruism?
checks.a: Integrity: honesty and acting by the code of ethics and standards. Altruism is concern for others’ welfare; this action is about truthfulness in the record.

checks.q: Which ANA provision is most directly involved when a nurse refuses a fourth consecutive 12-hour shift because she is too fatigued to practice safely?
checks.a: Provision 5: the nurse owes the same duties to self as to others, including promoting her own health and safety and preserving competence. It also protects clients (Provision 3).

checks.q: A client deciding about hospice says, “I always make decisions by talking to my pastor first, and I did again this time.” Which values-clarification step does this reflect?
checks.a: Act with a pattern: the decision aligns with how the client consistently makes choices. The nurse can affirm this and ask whether the client would make the same choice again.

checks.q: You see a nursing assistant mocking a client with schizophrenia in the hallway. Which value is violated, and what do you do?
checks.a: Human dignity (also ANA Provision 1). Intervene immediately and privately redirect the assistant, then report to the charge nurse per policy so the behavior is addressed; ensure the client is treated respectfully.

checks.q: Why is “I’m not allowed to share my opinion” a weaker response than redirecting to the client’s values?
checks.a: It closes communication and leaves the client without support. The goal is to support autonomy by helping the client explore alternatives and consequences, which requires keeping the conversation open.

topics.title: Ethical Principles, Diversity & Ethical Decision Making
topics.summary: Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, and veracity, together with advocacy, confidentiality, and informed consent, are the principles the nurse balances at the bedside, always considering the client first and using a systematic process (and the ethics committee) when they collide.
objectives: Define and apply autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, and veracity to bedside situations, and recognize which principle drives a given nursing action.
Recognize when two principles conflict (for example, autonomy vs beneficence) and choose the action that best balances them with the client’s wishes.
Advocate for informed consent, capacity, and the client’s right to refuse, presuming capacity unless there is clear evidence otherwise.
Protect confidentiality and PHI under the HIPAA Privacy Rule in phone, electronic, and in-person situations.
Provide culturally and religiously respectful care by assessing the individual client’s beliefs rather than stereotyping.
Protect vulnerable populations (children, pregnant people, prisoners, older adults, people with cognitive impairment) from coercion and undue influence.
Use a systematic ethical decision-making process and identify when to involve the interdisciplinary ethics committee.
topics.bigPicture:
Ethical principles are not philosophy-class abstractions; they are the reasons behind dozens of routine nursing decisions. You hold an opioid when respirations drop (nonmaleficence). You explain a procedure fully before the consent is signed (autonomy and veracity). You give the same careful pain assessment to the client from the shelter as to the client in the VIP suite (justice). When you refuse to tell a caller whether someone is in the ED, you are protecting confidentiality, which is both an ethical duty and a legal one under HIPAA.

The hard part is that principles collide. A client with uncontrolled hypertension refuses daily medication: her autonomy says respect it; beneficence says prevent a stroke. A family asks you not to tell their mother her diagnosis: their love says protect her; veracity and autonomy say she has a right to know. The NCLEX rarely asks you to pick a winner in the abstract. It asks for the action that respects the client’s wishes while still doing good: assess why, inform fully, remove barriers, involve the team, and escalate to the ethics committee when the conflict cannot be resolved.

Your anchor on every one of these items is Provision 2 of the ANA Code: the nurse’s primary commitment is to the client. You owe duties to the provider, the facility, and your own conscience, but the client comes first, balanced with the client’s wishes and the family’s desires.

keyTerms.def: A person who expresses and defends the cause of another person.

Supporting and defending the client’s rights, safety, health, and wishes, especially when illness limits the client’s ability to assert them; includes ensuring the client has enough information for informed consent and an environment that supports autonomous decisions.
The right to self-determination; respecting a client’s right to make health care decisions, including refusing treatment, even when the nurse disagrees.
Taking positive action to promote good, because the basic obligation of health care providers is to help others.
The obligation to do no harm and to safeguard clients. Intentional harm is never acceptable; when an intervention carries unavoidable risk, the risk of harm is weighed against the potential benefit.

Fairness: treating all clients fairly and in accordance with honor, standards, or law. Commonly arises in allocating scarce resources (staff, organs, protective equipment) and in giving equal time and care to every client.
Telling the truth; giving clients complete, honest information about their illness and treatment options, even when family asks to withhold it, so clients can give true informed consent.
The ethical and legal obligation to keep client information private, sharing it only with those who need it to provide care or as the client authorizes or law requires.

Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, individually identifiable health information (including the fact that a person is a client) held or transmitted by a covered entity in any form: electronic, paper, or oral.

A capable client’s voluntary agreement after the provider explains the procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives (including no treatment). The provider obtains it; the nurse commonly witnesses the signature and advocates if the client does not understand.

The clinical ability to understand information, appreciate its consequences, reason, and communicate a choice. Capacity is presumed unless clear evidence or documentation shows otherwise; competence is the related legal determination made by a court.

A legal document (for example, a living will or health care power of attorney) that states the client’s wishes or names a decision-maker if the client becomes unable to decide; it protects self-determination.
Overriding or bypassing a client’s choices “for their own good”; the opposite of respecting autonomy and the classic wrong answer on ethics items.

Groups with limited autonomy who are especially susceptible to coercion, undue influence, and abuse, particularly in research: children, pregnant people, prisoners, older adults, and people with cognitive impairments.

A team that helps ensure ethical care, assists when clients cannot express their wishes, mediates conflicts between client or family and the provider or facility, and serves as a supportive resource for routine ethical questions.

sections.heading: The core principles, explained by what they make you do
sections.body:
Each principle answers a different question. Autonomy: Whose decision is it? (The capable client’s.) Beneficence: What will actively help? Nonmaleficence: What could harm, and is the risk worth the benefit? Justice: Is this fair to this client and to others who need the same resources? Veracity: Am I telling the whole truth? Your course names autonomy, beneficence, justice, and veracity as the four primary principles “alongside nonmaleficence”; standard bioethics lists the big four as autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Learn all five; the NCLEX uses all five, plus fidelity (keeping promises), which you will meet in Exemplar 44.A.

Notice how beneficence and nonmaleficence differ. Beneficence is a positive duty (do something good: turn the client, teach, relieve pain). Nonmaleficence is a restraining duty (do not harm: hold the medication, use a safe technique, do not restrain unnecessarily). When a stem describes the nurse not doing something to prevent harm, think nonmaleficence; when it describes doing something to help, think beneficence.

check.q: A nurse checks the platelet count and holds a scheduled enoxaparin dose when the count has dropped sharply, then calls the provider. Which principle is primarily guiding her?
check.a: Nonmaleficence: she is refraining from an action that could cause harm (bleeding). Beneficence would describe a positive action to promote good.

sections.heading: Autonomy, capacity, and informed consent
sections.body:
Autonomy only works if the client has information and capacity. Advocacy means making sure medical staff clearly explain interventions, discussing the plan of care, allowing self-determination, and recognizing the client’s right to refuse treatment and procedures.

The provider performing the procedure obtains informed consent: explaining the procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives, including no treatment. The nurse usually witnesses the signature, verifying that the client is the person signing, is signing voluntarily, and appears to understand. If the client says, “I don’t really know what they’re doing,” the nurse does not explain the surgery herself or let the client sign anyway; the nurse holds the consent and notifies the provider to re-explain. Consent must be voluntary: no coercion, no rushing, no sedating medications that impair understanding before signing.

Capacity is presumed in adults. Clients with developmental disabilities or cognitive impairments may lack capacity for some decisions and may need protection from abuse, but a diagnosis alone does not remove the right to decide. Assess capacity for the specific decision, communicate in an accessible way (plain language, pictures, extra time), know whether a legal guardian exists and the limits of that guardianship, and advocate when cognitive deficits put the client’s rights in jeopardy.

Protecting vulnerable populations. The safety alert in this module is about research, but the principle applies everywhere. Children, pregnant people, prisoners, older adults, and people with cognitive impairments often have limited autonomy, which makes them especially vulnerable to coercion (threats or pressure), undue influence (excessive rewards or authority pressure), and abuse. A prisoner told that participating “will look good to the parole board,” a laboring client asked to sign a research consent between contractions, or an older adult with dementia enrolled without a legally authorized representative are all red flags. The nurse’s role is to protect the voluntary nature of consent, ensure the person or legally authorized representative understands, honor the right to withdraw at any time without penalty, and report concerns to the investigator or institutional review board.

Two consent situations the exam loves. Emergencies: when a client cannot consent and delay would threaten life or limb, consent is implied and treatment proceeds; the reason is documented. This exception does not override a valid, known refusal such as a documented advance directive. Refusal by a capable client: the client may refuse any treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, and may leave against medical advice. Work through it step by step: (1) confirm the client has capacity for this decision; (2) ask what the client understands and why he is refusing, because fear, cost, pain, or misinformation can often be fixed; (3) make sure the provider explains the risks of refusing and the alternatives; (4) respect the informed decision, without threats, guilt, or repeated pressure; (5) notify the provider, document the client’s own words and the teaching given, and follow facility policy (for example, a refusal or AMA form); and (6) keep caring for the client and leave the door open if he changes his mind. Restraining or sedating a capable adult to give care he refused is battery, not advocacy.
sections.example: A 34-year-old client with Down syndrome lives in a group home and makes her own medical decisions. Her mother, who is not her legal guardian, arrives and says she will sign the consent for a colonoscopy. The nurse explains that the client is her own decision-maker, asks the provider to explain the procedure to the client in simple language with pictures, and checks understanding with teach-back. The mother is welcome to support her daughter if the daughter wishes.

check.q: A client who received IV morphine 20 minutes ago is asked to sign a surgical consent. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Do not proceed with witnessing; notify the provider. A sedating medication may impair understanding, so consent may not be valid. Follow facility policy on timing of consent after sedatives.

sections.heading: Veracity and the family who asks you to keep a secret
sections.body:
Veracity requires complete, honest information so the client can give true informed consent. When family members ask the team to withhold a diagnosis, the nurse does not lie, does not agree to deceive, and does not deliver the bad news alone outside the nurse’s role. Instead, the nurse acknowledges the family’s fear, explains that the client has the right to information about his or her own health, and ensures the provider discusses the results with the client.

The key nuance is that information belongs to the client, and the client decides how much to know and who else should know. Some clients, often for cultural reasons, prefer that a family member receive information and make decisions. That is an autonomous choice when the client makes it. So the best first step is often to ask the client: “How much would you like to know about your results, and who would you like involved?” Never accept the family’s word for what the client wants.
sections.example: A son tells the nurse, “Don’t tell Dad it’s cancer; it will kill him.” Later the father asks the nurse, “Is it cancer? Nobody will give me a straight answer.” Best response: “You have every right to know your results. I will ask your doctor to come and go over them with you today; would you like anyone with you?” The nurse then informs the provider and supports the son separately.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and HIPAA
sections.body:
Nurses are ethically obligated to protect confidentiality at all times and in all settings, and the HIPAA Privacy Rule makes it law. PHI includes far more than diagnoses: the very fact that a person is (or was) a client is protected. Key practices: limit electronic chart access to authorized staff with a need to know; never look up a client who is not in your care (including family, friends, celebrities, or yourself through the work system); log off workstations; never discuss clients in elevators, cafeterias, or on social media, even “without names”; and follow institutional privacy policies.

The classic NCLEX phone call: someone claiming to be an employer, relative, or friend calls and asks whether a person was treated today. The nurse cannot confirm or deny that the person is a client. The calm, correct response is that the nurse cannot share information about who is or is not a client and suggests the caller contact the person directly. Asking the caller to prove identity does not solve the problem; even a verified employer has no right to PHI without the client’s authorization. Information may be shared with others involved in care (oncoming nurse, provider, consulting therapist) as needed for treatment.

When confidentiality is lawfully overridden. Confidentiality is strong but not absolute. Information may be shared without the client’s authorization when the law requires it: mandatory reports of suspected child abuse, abuse or neglect of vulnerable adults, and certain communicable diseases to the health department, a court order, or a serious and imminent threat of harm to an identifiable person. In those cases, share only the minimum necessary with the designated agency, never with curious callers, co-workers who are not involved, or social media. If you are unsure whether a disclosure is allowed, do not guess: ask the privacy officer or charge nurse.

check.q: A caller says she is the client’s sister and gives the client’s birthdate correctly. The client has not listed anyone as authorized. What does the nurse say?
check.a: The nurse cannot confirm or share information. Knowing a birthdate does not establish the client’s permission. The nurse can offer to take a message without confirming the person is there, per policy, or suggest the caller contact the person directly.

sections.heading: Advance directives, comfort, and teaching as ethical duties
sections.body:
Advance directives protect self-determination when a client can no longer speak. Discuss them before surgery and procedures, place copies in the record, and make sure they are followed if the client becomes incapacitated. If a family member demands treatment the client refused in a valid directive, the nurse advocates for the client by bringing the directive to the provider’s attention and involving the ethics committee if the conflict persists.

Comfort raises justice questions. Clients with chronic pain often face inadequate access to pain resources, and high health care use raises resource-allocation concerns. Nurses must relieve pain while minimizing risk of misuse: become educated about chronic pain, set realistic expectations with the client, refer to pain specialists, address personal biases about opioid use, and monitor for signs of misuse. Labeling a client as “drug-seeking” without assessment violates justice and beneficence.

Teaching and learning is an ethical duty because early discharges mean clients must manage complex self-care at home. Assess learning needs and abilities at the first encounter, use appropriate methods and materials, set aside personal biases, and verify comprehension (teach-back). Teaching that the client cannot understand does not support autonomy.

sections.heading: Religion, culture, and diversity without stereotyping
sections.body: Because the U.S. population is increasingly diverse, nurses often care for clients whose religious or cultural beliefs differ from their own about end-of-life care, reproduction, or blood transfusion. Three principles prevent conflict. First, identify common ground: most religions share values like helping the less fortunate, taking responsibility for one’s actions, and treating others as you wish to be treated. Second, assess the individual: not every person follows every tenet of their religion. Many Catholics, for example, find birth control or certain end-of-life choices acceptable despite official teaching; some Jehovah’s Witnesses accept certain blood fractions or cell-salvage techniques. Ask; do not assume. Third, honor autonomy throughout care, unless the client’s choice forces the nurse to act against the nurse’s own deeply held moral beliefs; then the nurse seeks guidance from the supervisor or ethics committee to arrange a safe transfer of care without abandoning the client.
sections.example: A client who identifies as a Jehovah’s Witness is scheduled for hip replacement. Rather than writing “refuses all blood” on the plan, the nurse asks, “Some people in your faith accept certain blood products or blood-saving techniques and others do not. What is acceptable to you?” The client accepts albumin and cell salvage but refuses red cells. The nurse documents the specific choices and makes sure the surgical team knows.

sections.heading: A systematic ethical decision-making process
sections.body:
The goal of ethical reasoning is a rational, systematic decision, never one based only on emotion, intuition, fixed rules, or precedent. It incorporates the client’s strengths and needs, evidence-based care, and the integrity of the client, nurse, and team. Applying Provision 2 starts with self-awareness: What do I know about this client’s clinical situation? What are the client’s values? What are my biases and assumptions? What is my primary obligation to this client?

Figure 44.1 summarizes the goal: client advocacy + client + family + health care team = optimal outcome. The nurse owes duties to the client, the provider, the employer, and personal ethics, but considers the client first, balanced with the client’s wishes and family desires. Moral distress from frequent ethical conflict is real; use mentors, colleagues, spiritual advisors, and the ethics committee.
steps: Gather the facts: clinical data, the client’s capacity, stated wishes, advance directives, and who the legal decision-maker is.
Identify the ethical problem and which principles conflict (for example, autonomy vs beneficence).
Clarify values: the client’s, the family’s, the team’s, and your own biases.
Identify options, including the consequences of each, and who has the authority to decide.
Choose the option that best meets the client’s needs and wishes; involve the ethics committee if conflict persists.
Act, communicate, and document.
Evaluate the outcome and reflect; seek support for moral distress.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: principle conflicts and best responses
sections.body:
Patterns: (1) “Which principle is the nurse demonstrating?”: translate the action into do good, avoid harm, respect choice, be fair, or tell the truth. (2) “Best response” to a family secret or a privacy request. (3) “First action” when consent or capacity is in doubt: stop and notify the provider. (4) SATA about HIPAA or advocacy behaviors. (5) Conflicts that need the ethics committee.

Sample question: A client with capacity who has advanced COPD tells the nurse she does not want to be intubated again. Her daughter says, “Mom isn’t thinking clearly. If she gets worse, I want everything done.” The client has no written advance directive. Which action should the nurse take first? (A) Tell the daughter that the client has the right to refuse and the matter is closed. (B) Notify the provider so the client’s wishes can be discussed and documented, including code status. (C) Ask the chaplain to help the daughter accept her mother’s decision. (D) Document that the daughter will make decisions if the client deteriorates.
steps: Read the stem: a capable client states a treatment refusal; a family member disagrees; nothing is in writing yet.
Identify the ask: the first action that best protects the client’s autonomy.
Spot the cues: “with capacity” means the client decides; “no written advance directive” means the wish is at risk of being lost if she deteriorates.
Eliminate A: autonomy is correct, but the response is dismissive and does nothing to secure the client’s wish in the record.
Eliminate C: supporting the daughter may help later, but it does not protect the client’s decision now.
Eliminate D: it hands authority to the daughter while the client is capable, which undermines autonomy.
Choose B: the provider must discuss goals of care and write code-status orders; the nurse advocates by getting the client’s wish formally documented (and can offer advance-directive information).

check.a: Find the person who has the right to decide (the capable client), then pick the action that protects that person’s informed choice through the right channel (provider, documentation, ethics committee) rather than an action that argues, persuades, or transfers decision-making to someone else.

sections.heading: Worked case: the sixth ED visit
sections.body: Ms. Rivera, 52, arrives at the ED with a severe headache and BP 212/108 mm Hg. It is her sixth visit for the same problem. She never filled her prescribed antihypertensive. She says she walks every day instead because “I can’t keep missing work for all those appointments.” After she is stabilized, a woman identifying herself as her manager calls the ED asking whether Ms. Rivera was seen today and when she will be back at work.
steps: Recognize the ethical tension: autonomy (she chose not to take the medication) vs beneficence and nonmaleficence (uncontrolled BP risks stroke, MI, kidney damage).

Assess before teaching: health literacy, her beliefs about hypertension and medications, and barriers to adherence. Telling her “you could have a stroke” without understanding why she stopped is ineffective and paternalistic.
Analyze: the barrier is social and economic (fear of losing work time), not lack of caring; walking is a strength to build on.

Generate solutions with her: ask the provider about a once-daily regimen and arrange a bedside phone consult with her primary provider and a clinical nurse specialist to build an outpatient BP plan (home BP monitoring, telehealth, evening appointments). This maximizes beneficence while supporting her autonomy in self-management through interprofessional collaboration.
Include her in discharge planning, along with her primary provider and outpatient support, and verify understanding with teach-back.

Handle the phone call: remain calm, do not confirm or deny that she is a client, and suggest the caller contact Ms. Rivera directly. This is the HIPAA Privacy Rule and the ethical duty of confidentiality.
Evaluate: she states her plan in her own words, has a follow-up she can attend, and decides what to tell her employer herself.

check.q: Why is “Can you confirm your name and employee ID so I can verify you?” the wrong response to the caller?
check.a: Verifying identity does not create a right to the information. Without the client’s authorization, the nurse cannot even confirm the client is in the department.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Advance directives in North Carolina include the Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3), which names a health care agent, and the Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (the NC living will, G.S. 90-321). The state’s portable medical order form for seriously ill clients is the MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment), which travels with the client across settings.

Minor consent (G.S. 90-21.5): a minor may give effective consent for services for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of sexually transmitted and other reportable diseases; pregnancy (but not sterilization or abortion); abuse of controlled substances or alcohol; and emotional disturbance. Emancipated minors may consent. The age of majority is 18. In practice, an adolescent seeking STI testing can consent to it, and that care is generally kept confidential. This matches the national NCLEX rule: every state lets minors consent to STI care.

Mandatory reporting protects vulnerable clients: North Carolina is a universal reporting state for child maltreatment (G.S. 7B-301): any person who suspects a juvenile is abused, neglected, or dependent must report to the county department of social services (DSS). Any person with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to county DSS (G.S. 108A-102). Good-faith reporters are immune. Reporting is one of the times confidentiality is lawfully overridden.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 44 study guide, pp. 2732–2737 (Outcome 44.2 Concepts Related to Ethics and Diversity and the related-concepts table; Outcome 44.4 Principles and Practices of Ethical Decision Making, Safety Alert, Figure 44.1; Outcome 44.5 ethics committees; Case Study June D’Angelo Parts 1–3).

Clarifications: (1) The course lists the four primary principles as autonomy, beneficence, justice, and veracity, “alongside nonmaleficence.” Standard bioethics (Beauchamp and Childress) names autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice as the four core principles; veracity and fidelity are additional principles. Learn all of them. (2) The course says ethics committees are “mandated by The Joint Commission.” More precisely, The Joint Commission requires accredited hospitals to have a process for addressing ethical issues; most hospitals meet this with an ethics committee or ethics consultation service. (3) Veracity is owed to the client, and a capable client may choose to receive less information or delegate it to family; the nurse confirms that choice with the client, not the family. (4) The worked case uses a new client to illustrate the same reasoning as the June D’Angelo case.

mnemonics.name: “Am Being Never Just Vague”
mnemonics.text: Autonomy (respect choice), Beneficence (do good), Nonmaleficence (no harm), Justice (be fair), Veracity (tell the truth).

mnemonics.name: HIPAA phone rule: “Can’t confirm, can’t deny, contact them directly”
mnemonics.text: For any caller without client authorization, the nurse neither confirms nor denies the person is a client and suggests contacting the person directly.

pearls: The capable client is the decision-maker; family members support but do not override.
Presume capacity in adults, including those with disabilities, unless clear evidence or documentation shows otherwise.
If the client does not understand a procedure at consent, the nurse stops and notifies the provider; the nurse does not explain the surgery or witness anyway.
The fact that someone is a client is PHI: never confirm or deny to an unauthorized caller.
Ask the individual what their religion or culture means for their care; never assume all members of a faith share every belief.
Assess barriers and beliefs before teaching; “noncompliance” often has a fixable cause.
Request an ethics consultation when the client or family and the team cannot resolve a values conflict, or as support for routine ethical questions.
redFlags: A family request to deceive the client or to sign for a capable client.
A consent signed by a client who is sedated, confused, or says they do not understand.
Different quality of pain management based on assumptions about “drug-seeking.”
Research enrollment involving coercion, undue influence, or no legally authorized representative for a client lacking capacity.
Anyone accessing a chart without a care relationship, or client information shared in public spaces or social media.
recap: Autonomy respects choice, beneficence does good, nonmaleficence avoids harm, justice is fairness, and veracity is truth.
When principles conflict, choose the action that protects the capable client’s informed choice while still pursuing benefit.
Advocacy is ensuring information, capacity, and the right to refuse, even when the nurse disagrees.
HIPAA protects all identifiable information, including the fact of being a client.
Assess the individual’s beliefs; avoid stereotyping; transfer care safely if your conscience truly forbids participation.
Vulnerable groups need extra protection from coercion and undue influence.
Ethical decisions are systematic, client-centered, and supported by the ethics committee when needed.

checks.q: A capable client with a gangrenous foot refuses amputation. The surgeon asks the nurse to “keep working on him.” What is the nurse’s role?
checks.a: Advocate for autonomy: ensure he has complete information about risks, benefits, and alternatives, explore his reasons and fears, and respect his informed refusal. Persuasion and repeated pressure are paternalistic. Document and notify the provider of his decision.

checks.q: A charge nurse assigns the most experienced nurse to the client whose family “complains the most” rather than to the most unstable client. Which principle is at stake?
checks.a: Justice: allocation of a scarce resource (nursing expertise) should be based on client need, not on who is most demanding.

checks.q: An adult client with moderate dementia keeps removing her oxygen. Her daughter is her health care agent. A research coordinator wants to enroll her in a study today. What should the nurse check?
checks.a: Whether the client can consent and, if not, that the legally authorized representative gives informed, voluntary consent; that the client’s assent and objections are respected; and that there is no coercion or undue influence. Report concerns to the investigator or IRB.

checks.q: A client asks the nurse, “Am I dying? My wife says I’m getting better.” What principle applies and what is the best response?
checks.a: Veracity and autonomy. Explore what he understands and wants to know, then ensure the provider discusses his condition honestly with him; do not offer false reassurance or confirm the wife’s account to deceive him.

checks.q: A nurse is caring for a client with sickle cell crisis whom a colleague calls “a frequent flyer.” What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Set aside the bias, assess pain with a valid tool, administer prescribed analgesia promptly, reassess, and advocate for a pain plan. This upholds beneficence and justice.

checks.q: Why is calling the ethics committee not a sign of failure?
checks.a: Ethics committees mediate conflicts and assist when clients cannot express wishes, and evidence supports using them as a supportive resource for routine ethical decisions, not only for major disputes.

topics.title: Exemplar 44.A Morality: Moral Frameworks, Dilemmas & Accountability
topics.summary: Morality is the personal sense of right and wrong; this exemplar teaches you to recognize a true moral dilemma, reason through it with consequence-, principle-, and relationship-based frameworks, and practice with fidelity, accountability, and responsibility.
objectives: Recognize the cues that a situation is moral (guilt, shame, hope; ought, should, right, wrong) and apply the four criteria to decide whether a true moral dilemma exists.
Differentiate consequence-based (teleologic), principles-based (deontologic), and relationship-based (caring) moral frameworks, and identify which one a nurse’s reasoning reflects.
Apply utilitarianism and the principle of utility to triage and scarce-resource decisions.
Demonstrate fidelity, accountability, and responsibility in everyday nursing actions, including error disclosure.
Recognize moral distress and select evidence-based individual and organizational strategies to manage it.
Respond to a client whose care has been compromised by another nurse’s bias or miscommunication, as in the Keith Morgan case.
Choose individual and unit-level strategies that improve the ethical climate and support ethical practice.
topics.bigPicture:
Morality is the part of ethics that lives inside each person. It is the uneasy feeling when a promise cannot be kept, the guilt after an error, the anger when a client is treated unfairly. Those feelings are useful signals: they tell you a moral issue is present. But feelings are not a decision method. This exemplar teaches you how to move from “this feels wrong” to a rational, defensible action.

Not every hard day is a moral dilemma. A medication you are unsure how to dose is a knowledge problem: look it up or ask. A visiting-hours policy is a policy question. A true moral dilemma requires competing moral principles, competing needs, the freedom to choose, and a decision shaped by feelings and the situation. When those conditions are met, frameworks help: consequence-based thinking asks which outcome is best, principle-based thinking asks which duty must be honored, and relationship-based thinking asks what caring for these particular people requires.

Finally, morality in nursing is about character in action: fidelity (keeping promises), accountability (answering for your choices, including your mistakes), and responsibility (reliably doing your job). On the NCLEX these appear as error-disclosure priority questions, promise-keeping scenarios, mandatory reporting, and the end-of-chapter case in which a client is suffering because another nurse let personal bias override the prescribed plan.

sections.heading: Recognizing a moral issue
sections.body:
Moral issues concern important social values and norms, not trivial preferences. Whether a client gets a turkey or ham sandwich is not a moral issue; whether a client is told the truth about a prognosis is. Two kinds of clues signal a moral situation. Feelings: guilt, shame, hope, and indignation. Language: ought, should, right, wrong, good, bad. When you hear yourself say, “We should tell him,” or feel guilty leaving a client in pain, a moral issue is present.

Recognizing a moral issue is the first step, not the last. Personal morality differs from person to person, so “It just feels wrong to me” cannot be the justification for a nursing action. The nurse moves from moral feeling to ethical reasoning: Which principles apply? What are the facts? Who decides? This connects back to the ethics-vs-morality distinction from Outcome 44.1: your private morals alert you; professional ethics guide you.
sections.example: A nurse feels uneasy when a surgeon tells a client, “This is a minor procedure, nothing to worry about,” when the consent form lists a 10% risk of permanent nerve damage. The feeling (unease) and the thought (“He should know the real risk”) are moral cues. The nurse’s professional action is to ask the client what he understands and notify the surgeon that the client may not have full information before the consent is signed.

sections.heading: When is it a true moral dilemma? The four criteria
sections.body:
Many problems feel like dilemmas but are really knowledge gaps, policy questions, or communication problems that standard practice already answers. A true moral dilemma exists only when all four criteria are met. When they are met, the nurse uses structured ethical reasoning. When they are not, the nurse follows standard professional practice guidelines.

How to apply the criteria without getting tricked. Work through them in order and stop at the first “no.” (1) Do the possible actions pull different people in different directions? (2) Can you name two principles that point opposite ways? (3) Is there real freedom to choose, or does a law, a clear standard, or a policy already tell you what to do? (4) Are feelings and the specifics of the situation shaping the choice? Criterion 3 is where most exam distractors fail: mandatory reporting, holding an unsafe dose, and following a policy all remove freedom. Be careful, though: a law can settle part of a situation (for example, you may not disclose a client’s health information without permission) while still leaving a genuine choice about how to act within it.
steps: Potential solutions or actions conflict with the needs of one or more individuals (what helps one person harms or frustrates another).
One or more conflicting moral or ethical principles apply (for example, veracity vs fidelity, or autonomy vs beneficence).
There is freedom to make a decision (the nurse or team actually has a choice; it is not dictated by law or a clear standard).
The decision about which course to take is influenced by personal feelings and by the situation itself.

check.q: A nurse is torn about whether to report a colleague who documented vital signs she did not take. Is this a true moral dilemma?
check.a: Not really. Feelings are involved, but professional standards (integrity, client safety, duty to report falsification) give a clear answer, so the nurse follows standard practice and reports through the chain of command. Strong feelings alone do not make a dilemma.

sections.heading: Consequence-based (teleologic) theories and utilitarianism
sections.body:
Teleologic theories (from the Greek telos, end) judge an action entirely by its outcome. The question is “Which action produces the best result?” Utilitarianism is the most familiar version: the moral act is the one that produces the greatest good for the greatest number while harming the fewest. Its rule, the principle of utility, is applied when resources, medications, or treatments are limited.

You already use utilitarian reasoning in disaster triage: in a mass-casualty event, staff and supplies go first to those who will benefit most, and the expectant client who cannot survive receives comfort care rather than all the resources. Public health uses it too: quarantine limits individual freedom to protect many. The weakness of pure consequence-based reasoning is that it can justify harming one person if the total outcome is better, which is why it is balanced with duties and rights (you would never harvest one client’s organs to save five).
sections.analogy: Teleologic thinking is like a coach choosing plays by the scoreboard: whatever wins the game is the right play. Deontologic thinking is like a referee: some rules cannot be broken even if breaking them would win the game.

check.q: During a pandemic, a hospital allocates its last ventilators using a clinical score that predicts who is most likely to survive with treatment. Which framework is this?
check.a: Consequence-based (teleologic) reasoning using utilitarianism and the principle of utility: limited resources are allocated to produce the greatest good for the greatest number. Applying the same criteria to everyone also serves justice.

sections.heading: Principles-based (deontologic) theories
sections.body:
Deontologic theories (from the Greek deon, duty) hold that an action is right when it fulfills a moral duty or rule, regardless of consequences. The philosopher most linked to this view is Immanuel Kant. Duties such as “tell the truth,” “keep promises,” “never use a person merely as a means,” and “respect persons” bind you even if breaking them would produce a better outcome in a given case.

Nursing’s principles (autonomy, veracity, fidelity, nonmaleficence) are largely deontologic: you tell a client the truth because truthfulness is owed, not because you calculated it would make the client happier. Mandatory reporting laws and codes of ethics also function as duties. The weakness: duties can conflict with each other (fidelity vs veracity) and following a rule rigidly can ignore context, which is where relationship-based thinking helps.
sections.example: A nurse says, “Even though the family thinks the truth will upset her, I won’t lie to her when she asks. Lying is wrong, whatever happens.” This is deontologic reasoning: the duty of veracity governs regardless of the consequence.

sections.heading: Relationship-based (caring) theories
sections.body:
Relationship-based or caring theories, associated with the ethics-of-care work of Carol Gilligan and Nel Noddings and with nursing caring theorists, place the relationship at the center. Instead of asking only “What rule applies?” or “What outcome is best?”, the nurse asks “What does caring for this particular person, in this situation, with these relationships, require?” Empathy, context, attentiveness, and responsiveness are the tools.

Caring theories explain many nursing decisions that rules alone do not: adjusting how and when bad news is delivered to a client whose family structure and fears you understand, involving a client’s chosen family, or advocating for a client who feels unheard. They do not replace principles. A caring nurse still tells the truth, but she tells it with attention to timing, setting, support, and the client’s readiness.

check.a: Relationship-based (caring): the decision flows from the relationship, empathy, and the specific context, not from a rule or an outcome calculation.

sections.heading: Fidelity, accountability, and responsibility in practice
sections.body:
Fidelity is keeping promises and remaining faithful to commitments. Small promises matter: “I’ll be back in 15 minutes with your pain medication.” If you are delayed by an emergency, fidelity means arranging for a colleague to bring the medication or letting the client know about the delay, not silently breaking the promise. Do not make promises you cannot keep (for example, “I promise nothing bad will happen” or “I won’t tell anyone” about information you are legally required to report).

Accountability is answerability: explaining and owning your decisions and their consequences. After a medication error, accountability means first assessing the client, then notifying the provider, completing an event report per policy, and being honest. Hiding an error is the opposite of accountability and integrity. Responsibility is reliability and dependability in fulfilling duties: completing assessments on time, following through on orders, showing up for scheduled shifts. A simple way to separate them: responsibility is doing the job; accountability is answering for how you did it.

check.q: A nurse realizes she gave a client his 0900 metoprolol 3 hours early. List her actions in order.
check.a: First assess the client (heart rate, blood pressure, symptoms), then notify the provider, follow orders, document factually in the record, and complete an event report per policy. Honesty with the client is also expected per facility disclosure policy. Assessment comes first because client safety precedes paperwork.

sections.heading: Moral distress and strategies to enhance ethical practice
sections.body:
Frequent ethical issues cause moral distress and burnout. Evidence in your course shows: less experienced nurses encounter ethical dilemmas more often, and seeking advice from a mentor or experienced peer facilitates effective solutions; nurses who feel competent in ethical knowledge perceive their unit’s ethical climate more positively, while lack of ethics education and organizational support leads to moral distress and burnout. Ethics committees should be used not only for major disputes but as a supportive resource for guidance and reassurance in routine ethical decisions.

Individual strategies: know ethical principles and the ANA Code; examine personal values and biases to provide nonjudgmental care; pursue continuing ethics education; respect differing values among interprofessional colleagues; practice with hypothetical ethical scenarios; serve on the agency ethics committee; and ensure nursing is represented in institutional ethics policies. Organizational resources: interdisciplinary ethics committees and free evidence-based clinical practice guidelines, such as those from the Hartford Institute for Geriatric Nursing (advance directives, dementia care, sexual health in older adults) and ACOG.
bullets: Signs of moral distress: guilt, anger, frustration, avoiding certain clients, dreading work, physical exhaustion, wanting to leave the unit or profession.
Healthy responses: debrief with colleagues, talk with a mentor, use spiritual advisors, request an ethics consultation, attend ethics education.
Unhealthy responses: suppressing the issue, avoiding the client, cynicism, or quitting without addressing the cause.
