sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: frameworks, dilemmas, and accountability
sections.body:
Patterns: (1) A nurse’s statement, then “Which ethical framework does this reflect?”: look for outcome words (utility, most people), duty words (always, never, regardless), or relationship words (our relationship, this family). (2) “Which situation represents a moral dilemma?”: apply all four criteria and eliminate knowledge, policy, and legal-duty problems. (3) Error-disclosure priority items: assess the client first. (4) Promise or bias scenarios: fidelity, accountability, and correcting another nurse’s misinformation.

Sample question: A home health nurse visits a client 5 days after surgery for a fractured tibia. He rates his pain 8/10 and says, “The last nurse told me all I needed was acetaminophen, so I haven’t taken the oxycodone the doctor prescribed.” Which action should the nurse take first? (A) Call the agency supervisor to report the previous nurse. (B) Assess the client’s pain and his understanding of the prescribed regimen. (C) Tell the client to take the oxycodone now along with his acetaminophen. (D) Contact the provider to request a stronger prescription.
steps: Read the stem: severe pain, prescribed opioid not taken because of another nurse’s misinformation.
Identify the ask: the first action.
Spot cues: 8/10 pain (a client need), a knowledge deficit, and a communication/bias problem by a colleague.
Eliminate A: reporting the miscommunication per policy is required (accountability), but it does not address the client’s pain now and is not first.
Eliminate C: teaching before assessing could be unsafe (how much acetaminophen has he taken, allergies, sedation risk, other substances?).
Eliminate D: the existing prescription may be adequate; requesting a change before assessing is premature.

Choose B: assess pain characteristics, what he has taken, and what he understands; then teach accurately (veracity, beneficence), contact the provider to review the plan, and report per policy (accountability, integrity).

check.a: When a moral or professional problem coexists with a client need, address the client first, usually by assessing, then correct the information, then use the reporting channel. Paperwork and blame come after safety.

sections.heading: Worked case: the promise, the prognosis, and the partner
sections.body: Mr. Okafor, 71, has metastatic pancreatic cancer and capacity. Last week he told his nurse, “Please don’t tell my wife how bad it is yet; I want to tell her myself when the time is right,” and the nurse agreed. Today his wife tells the nurse she is about to sign a contract to sell their home and move out of state “once he’s better,” and asks, “He’s going to recover, isn’t he?”
steps: Recognize moral cues: the nurse feels guilt and conflict; she thinks the wife “should” know. A moral issue is present.

Test the four criteria: conflicting needs (his privacy vs her planning); conflicting principles (fidelity and confidentiality vs veracity toward the wife); freedom to choose how to respond (confidentiality rules already settle that the nurse may not reveal his prognosis without his permission, but they do not dictate what she says to the wife or how she helps him share the news); feelings and the situation influence the choice. This is a true moral dilemma about how to act, not about whether to disclose.

Apply frameworks: consequence-based thinking notes the harm of a major move based on false hope; deontologic thinking says the nurse must not lie and must keep confidences; caring thinking asks what this couple’s relationship needs.

Choose an action that honors all three: do not lie to the wife and do not disclose his prognosis without his permission. Say, “That is an important question to talk about with your husband and his doctor. I’ll let them know you’d like to talk today.”

Return to the client: tell Mr. Okafor that his wife is making major decisions and is asking about his prognosis; offer support to tell her now, with the provider, social worker, or chaplain present. This keeps faith with the promise while respecting his autonomy.
If conflict persists or the nurse feels distressed, consult a mentor or the ethics committee.
Evaluate: the couple has an honest conversation that he leads; the nurse documents and debriefs.

check.q: Why is “He is doing very well; don’t worry” unacceptable even though it keeps the promise?
check.a: It violates veracity by giving false reassurance and may cause serious harm to the wife’s decisions. Fidelity never requires lying; the nurse can keep the confidence without deceiving.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Accountability and Just Culture. NCBON uses a Just Culture-based Complaint Evaluation Tool that distinguishes human error (an inadvertent slip; the system response is consoling the nurse and fixing the system), at-risk behavior (a drift such as skipping barcode scanning because “it’s faster”; the response is coaching), and reckless behavior (conscious disregard of a substantial risk; the response is discipline). Conduct issues such as diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary violations, and confidentiality breaches are reported to the Board rather than handled only by the employer. Alternative-to-discipline programs exist for substance use.

When reporting is a duty, not a dilemma. North Carolina is a universal child-maltreatment reporting state (G.S. 7B-301): any person with cause to suspect abuse, neglect, or dependency of a juvenile under 18 must report to the county DSS director. Report suspicion; do not investigate or wait for proof. Knowingly failing to report is a crime, and good-faith reporters are immune. Suspected abuse or neglect of a disabled adult needing protective services is likewise reported to county DSS (G.S. 108A-102).

Moral but unpaid. The NC Good Samaritan law (G.S. 90-21.14) protects a person giving emergency care without compensation unless there is gross negligence, wanton conduct, or intentional wrongdoing; it does not cover care given in the normal course of paid employment.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 44 study guide, pp. 2736–2739 (Outcome 44.5 moral dilemma criteria and strategies; evidence-based findings on ethical support; Exemplar 44.A moral frameworks, pp. 2738–2739; Apply Your Knowledge: Keith Morgan case, p. 2738; glossary entries for fidelity, accountability, responsibility).

Clarifications: (1) The course glosses teleologic theories with the question “Was the action fair?” Consequence-based theories ask whether the outcome was good (the best balance of benefit over harm); fairness is the concern of justice. (2) The course uses “narcotic analgesic”; current clinical language is opioid analgesic. (3) The Hartford Institute is formally the Hartford Institute for Geriatric Nursing (ConsultGeri resources). (4) Moral distress is defined here using standard nursing literature because the course names it without a formal definition. (5) The sample NCLEX walkthrough adapts the Keith Morgan case with new details; the worked case is original.

mnemonics.name: True dilemma: “Two clashes, a choice, and feelings”
mnemonics.text: Needs clash, principles clash, there is freedom to choose, and feelings plus the situation shape the choice. All four must be present.

mnemonics.name: Frameworks: “Telos = Total, Deon = Duty, Caring = Connection”
mnemonics.text: Teleologic judges the outcome; deontologic judges the duty; relationship-based judges what the connection requires.

pearls: Strong feelings signal a moral issue but do not make it a dilemma; check all four criteria.
If the law or a clear standard dictates the action (abuse reporting, holding an unsafe dose), there is no dilemma; act.
Utilitarianism and the principle of utility are the frameworks of triage and scarce resources.
Duty words (always, never, regardless of outcome) point to deontology; outcome words point to teleology.
Fidelity never requires lying; you can keep a confidence and still be truthful.
After an error, assess the client first, then notify, then document and report.
Less experienced nurses benefit most from mentors and from using the ethics committee for routine support.
redFlags: Making promises you cannot keep, especially secrecy about information you must report.
Hiding, delaying, or minimizing an error.
A colleague’s personal bias (for example, about opioids) overriding a client’s prescribed plan and leaving the client in pain.
Signs of moral distress in yourself or peers (avoidance, cynicism, burnout) that are not being addressed.
Waiting for proof before reporting suspected child or vulnerable-adult maltreatment.
recap: Morality is personal; moral cues are feelings (guilt, shame, hope) and words (ought, should, right, wrong).
A true moral dilemma meets all four criteria; otherwise follow standard practice guidelines.
Teleologic theories judge outcomes; utilitarianism seeks the greatest good for the greatest number.
Deontologic theories judge duties regardless of outcome; caring theories center relationships and context.
Fidelity is keeping promises, accountability is answering for actions, and responsibility is dependable performance.
Moral distress is managed with mentors, colleagues, spiritual advisors, ethics education, and the ethics committee.
In the Keith Morgan case: assess, teach accurately, contact the provider, and report the miscommunication per policy.

checks.q: A nurse says, “I’ll give the last dose of IV immune globulin to the client most likely to benefit, because that saves the most lives overall.” Name the framework and one ethical safeguard.
checks.a: Consequence-based (utilitarian) reasoning using the principle of utility. A safeguard is using transparent, consistent clinical criteria applied to every client (justice), not social worth or ability to pay.

checks.q: A nurse promised a client she would be back at 1400 to help him walk, but a rapid response is called on another client. What does fidelity require?
checks.a: Ask a colleague to tell the client about the delay or help him walk, and follow up when she is free. Fidelity means honoring the commitment or communicating honestly when she cannot.

checks.q: Is a nurse’s uncertainty about whether to give a PRN antiemetic for nausea a moral dilemma?
checks.a: No. It is a clinical judgment question answered by assessment and standard practice. There are no conflicting moral principles.

checks.q: A nurse colleague routinely silences bed alarms without checking clients “because they always false alarm.” Under Just Culture, how is this classified and what response fits?
checks.a: At-risk behavior (a drift from safe practice due to perceived low risk); the response is coaching plus fixing system contributors such as alarm fatigue. Reckless disregard would call for discipline.

checks.q: A new graduate feels sick each time she cares for a client receiving aggressive treatment she believes is futile. What evidence-based steps help?
checks.a: Recognize moral distress; talk with a mentor or experienced peer, debrief with colleagues, request an ethics consultation, and pursue ethics education. Avoiding the client is not a solution.

checks.q: Which framework is reflected when a nurse refuses to falsify a restraint-check log even though the manager says the audit will otherwise fail?
checks.a: Deontologic: the duty of honesty (integrity) applies regardless of the consequence to the unit’s audit.
